final_proof:
For a map f : S₁ → S₂ and A ⊆ S₁, write f[A] for the direct image of A. Thus the restricted direct-image mapping is U ↦ f[U] for U ∈ τ₁. We use the definition that a homeomorphism is a bijection which is continuous and whose inverse is continuous.

(⇒) Assume (S₂, τ₂) is a topological space homeomorphic to T₁, and choose a homeomorphism f : (S₁, τ₁) → (S₂, τ₂). In particular, f is bijective. Let g = f⁻¹ : S₂ → S₁. If U ∈ τ₁, then f[U] = g⁻¹[U], where the right side denotes the inverse image of U under g. Because g is continuous, g⁻¹[U] ∈ τ₂. Hence the restricted direct-image mapping sends τ₁ into τ₂.

Moreover, if V ∈ τ₂, continuity of f gives f⁻¹[V] ∈ τ₁, and surjectivity of f gives f[f⁻¹[V]] = V. Thus every member of τ₂ is in the range of the restricted direct-image mapping. That restriction is therefore a surjection from τ₁ to τ₂, proving (1) and (2).

(⇐) Conversely, suppose there is a map f : S₁ → S₂ satisfying (1) and (2). Since the restriction in (2) is a map from τ₁ onto τ₂, we have

  U ∈ τ₁ ⇒ f[U] ∈ τ₂,                                      (a)

and

  V ∈ τ₂ ⇒ V = f[U] for some U ∈ τ₁.                       (b)

We first verify that τ₂ is a topology on S₂. Because ∅, S₁ ∈ τ₁, (a) gives ∅ = f[∅] ∈ τ₂ and S₂ = f[S₁] ∈ τ₂, where the latter equality uses surjectivity of f.

Let (Vᵢ)ᵢ∈I be any family of members of τ₂. Put Uᵢ = f⁻¹[Vᵢ]. For each i, (b) supplies Wᵢ ∈ τ₁ with Vᵢ = f[Wᵢ]. Since f is injective, f⁻¹[f[Wᵢ]] = Wᵢ, and hence Uᵢ = Wᵢ ∈ τ₁. Therefore ⋃ᵢ∈I Uᵢ ∈ τ₁. Direct images commute with arbitrary unions, so

  ⋃ᵢ∈I Vᵢ = ⋃ᵢ∈I f[Uᵢ] = f[⋃ᵢ∈I Uᵢ] ∈ τ₂

by (a). Thus τ₂ is closed under arbitrary unions.

If V, W ∈ τ₂, set U = f⁻¹[V] and Z = f⁻¹[W]. The preceding argument shows that U, Z ∈ τ₁. Hence U ∩ Z ∈ τ₁. Since f is injective, f[U ∩ Z] = f[U] ∩ f[Z], and therefore

  V ∩ W = f[U] ∩ f[Z] = f[U ∩ Z] ∈ τ₂.

Thus τ₂ contains ∅ and S₂ and is closed under arbitrary unions and binary intersections; by induction it is closed under all finite intersections. Hence (S₂, τ₂) is a topological space.

It remains to prove that f is a homeomorphism. If V ∈ τ₂, then by (b) there is U ∈ τ₁ such that V = f[U]. Bijectivity gives f⁻¹[V] = f⁻¹[f[U]] = U ∈ τ₁, so f is continuous. Let g = f⁻¹ : S₂ → S₁. For every U ∈ τ₁, the inverse image of U under g is g⁻¹[U] = f[U], which belongs to τ₂ by (a). Hence g is continuous. Since f is bijective and both f and its inverse are continuous, f is a homeomorphism. Therefore (S₂, τ₂) is a topological space homeomorphic to T₁, as required.
